title: "Practical work 2: a network application with TCP or UDP"
---

::: {.callout-warning}
Draft: the subject and the grading criteria may still change slightly
before the kickoff.
:::

## Overview

Network applications are everywhere: to chat, to play, to watch videos,
to send emails. In this practical work, you create your own, in a group.

Your network application is made of an **application protocol** and two
programs that communicate over the network with it: a **server** and a
**client**, written in Java. You define the protocol, and you choose the
transport protocol it uses: TCP, UDP, or both.

**You choose what the application does.** A chat, a chess game, a
shopping list, the simulation of an Internet of Things (IoT) network,
and so on. Be creative, but reasonable: the point is the protocol and
the network code.

This practical work puts into practice
[chapter 06](../chapters/06-application-protocols.qmd) (Application
protocols), the TCP & UDP programming chapters and the Network
concurrency chapter. The application is packaged and published with
Docker, as in [chapter 05](../chapters/05-docker.qmd).

## Objectives

- Define an application protocol, in a specification another team could
  implement.
- Implement the protocol as a client and a server, with TCP and/or UDP.
- Serve several clients at the same time.
- Package, publish and run the application with Docker.
- Explain your work.

## Demos

Two demos, shown at the kickoff, give an idea of a finished practical
work. Each one is a Maven project with picocli; the commands below are
run from the root of the demos repository.

### Demo 1: file transfer, with TCP

The server serves the files of its directory; the client lists and
downloads them in a REPL. The server serves several clients at the same
time, with a pool of threads.

Build the project, then run the application without any arguments:

```sh
./mvnw --projects practical-work-2-tcp-demo clean package
java -jar practical-work-2-tcp-demo/target/practical-work-2-tcp-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
```

```{.text filename="Console"}
Missing required subcommand
Usage: practical-work-2-tcp-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar [-hV] [COMMAND]
A simple file transfer application
  -h, --help      Show this help message and exit.
  -V, --version   Print version information and exit.
Commands:
  server  Start a TCP server to serve files
  client  Start a client to download files from a server
```

Start the server, in the directory of the files to serve:

```sh
java -jar practical-work-2-tcp-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar server -p 12345 -t 4
```

Start the client, in another terminal:

```sh
java -jar practical-work-2-tcp-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar client -p 12345
```

### Demo 2: weather station, with UDP

Sensors (thermometer, humidity, pressure) send their measures to
multicast groups, fire and forget: `239.0.0.1` for the temperature,
`239.0.0.2` for the pressure, `239.0.0.3` for the humidity, all on port
9876. The weather station joins the groups and keeps the measures. A
client asks the station, in unicast on port 1234, for all the measures
of a sensor or their average.

Build the project, then run the application without any arguments:

```sh
./mvnw --projects practical-work-2-udp-demo clean package
java -jar practical-work-2-udp-demo/target/practical-work-2-udp-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
```

```{.text filename="Console"}
Missing required subcommand
Usage: practical-work-2-udp-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar [-hV] [COMMAND]
DAI Weather Station
  -h, --help      Show this help message and exit.
  -V, --version   Print version information and exit.
Commands:
  thermometer-emitter      Emits temperature values.
  pressure-emitter         Emits pressure values.
  humidity-emitter         Emits humidity values.
  weather-station          Start an UDP multicast receiver
  weather-client           Start an UDP weather client
  list-network-interfaces  List all available network interfaces
```

Start the weather station, on the network interface of your machine
(`en0` on a Mac, `eth0` on Linux):

```sh
java -jar practical-work-2-udp-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar weather-station \
  -i en0 --port 9876 --server-port 1234
```

```{.text filename="Weather station"}
Multicast receiver started (127.0.0.1:9876)
Unicast receiver started (127.0.0.1:1234)
```

Start two sensors, each in its own terminal; each one sends a measure
every 10 seconds:

```sh
java -jar practical-work-2-udp-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar thermometer-emitter \
  --delay=0 --frequency 10000 -i en0 -p 9876
java -jar practical-work-2-udp-demo-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar pressure-emitter \
  --delay=0 --frequency 10000 -i en0 -p 9876
```

```{.text filename="Thermometer"}

Multicasting measure : 38.0 to 239.0.0.1:9876 on interface en0

Multicasting measure : 32.0 to 239.0.0.1:9876 on interface en0

```

## Groups

You work in groups of **two to three** students. You choose your
partners. If you have no partner, we assign you one.

To announce your group, open a **GitHub Discussion** in the
[course organization]({{< var discussions-url >}}), category *Show and
tell*, with:

- **Title**: `[DAI {{< var year >}} Class <A or C>] PW2 - <first name> <last name>, …`
- **Description**: a few lines about what your application will do.

::: {.callout-important}
Do this before the next course, even if your idea is not final. We
use it to plan the presentations, and to tell you early if the scope is
too small or too large.
:::

## What your application must do

- Follow an **application protocol you define**, in a specification
  with the four sections of
  [chapter 06](../chapters/06-application-protocols.qmd#writing-a-specification).
  The [SMS protocol]({{< var examples-url >}}/tree/main/06-application-protocols/sms-protocol)
  is a model.
- Offer two commands with picocli: one starts the **server**, the other
  the **client**.
- Give the client a **REPL** (Read-Eval-Print Loop): the user types
  commands and reads the answers without leaving the application.
- Accept **several clients at the same time** on the server. If you
  cannot find an idea where several clients make sense, ask us.
- Be **packaged with Docker** and published on GitHub Container
  Registry.
- Be **slightly more than the course examples**, and slightly different.
  No need to shoot for the moon.

## Presentations

- DAI-TIC-A: **Wednesday 02.12**.
- DAI-TIC-C: **Tuesday 01.12**.

Each group has **8 minutes** to present its application. Come 5 minutes
before your slot, with your computer. A video projector is available.

You are free to present as you like, but:

- show the client and the server **running**, including an error case.
- explain the **protocol** and the choices behind it, not every line of
  code.
- everyone speaks, and everyone can answer questions about the code.

The timeslots are published here once the groups are known.

## Grading

Each criterion is worth:

- **0 point**: missing, off topic, or showing very little understanding.
- **0.1 point**: partially there, unclear or incomplete.
- **0.2 point**: complete, correct, and showing a clear understanding.

Final grade: 25 criteria × 0.2 = 5 points, + 1 = **6 maximum**.

| Category | Criteria | Points | Weight |
|----------|----------|-------:|-------:|
| 1. Docker and GitHub Container Registry | 1 to 4 | 0.8 | 16% |
| 2. Application protocol | 5 to 12 | 1.6 | 32% |
| 3. Network programming | 13 to 18 | 1.2 | 24% |
| 4. Network concurrency | 19 to 20 | 0.4 | 8% |
| 5. Tests | 21 | 0.2 | 4% |
| 6. Presentation | 22 to 25 | 0.8 | 16% |

The good practices of PW1 (Git, GitHub, README, Maven) are expected,
and missing ones cost points: see the [Rules](#rules).

## How to test your protocol

As in PW1, test the logic, not the network: keep what the server does
with a message separate from the code that reads and writes the socket.
A simple way is a method that takes the line received and returns the
answer to send. The network code only reads lines, calls it, and writes
the answers.

The tests then need no server and no client. With the
[SMS protocol]({{< var examples-url >}}/tree/main/06-application-protocols/sms-protocol):

```java
@Test
void answersAnUnknownMessageWithAnError() {
  Session session = new Session();
  assertEquals("ERROR -1", session.handle("HELLO"));
}

@Test
void refusesListBeforeJoin() {
  Session session = new Session();
  assertEquals("ERROR -2", session.handle("LIST"));
}
```

## Rules

Your practical work must respect the following rules.

**The team**

- Everyone contributes to the project, and the history shows it.
- Everyone can explain the whole project in detail if we ask, not only
  the part they wrote.

**The project**

- A GitHub Discussion is opened **before the next course**, so that we
  can validate your idea.
- The network communication uses only the **Java classes of the
  course**. Any other library may serve the rest of the application,
  the user interface for example. The README says which dependencies
  you use, and why.
- The application does **slightly more, and something slightly
  different**, than the examples shown in the course.
- The good practices of PW1 continue: issues, reviewed pull requests,
  descriptive and signed commits, the Maven wrapper, a clean
  `.gitignore`, and a README that explains how to build and run the
  application.
- The application **builds and runs from a fresh clone**, with
  `./mvnw clean package`, on a machine that is not yours. What we cannot
  build, we cannot grade.

**The submission**

- The Discussion is updated with the **repository link and the commit
  hash** before the deadline. We grade that commit, not what comes
  after it.
- If the repository is **private**, the teaching staff are
  collaborators. If we cannot open it at the deadline, the work counts
  as not submitted.
- Every started day of delay costs **1 point**.

**Honesty**

- State your sources: code from the internet, code generated by an AI
  tool, ideas taken elsewhere. Say what you used them for. See the
  [AI principles](../resources.qmd).
- Copying the code of another group gives a grade of **1** to everyone
  involved.

::: {.callout-caution}
These rules are not decoration. Not respecting one of them costs up to
**1 point** on the final grade, and several of them can add up.
:::

## Grades and feedback

Your grade goes into GAPS, and you receive an email with a comment for
each criterion, a general comment on your work, and the grade. If
anything is unclear, ask us.

## Tips

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Keep it simple"}
Remember the Unix philosophy and the KISS principle from PW1: *keep it
simple, silly*. A small protocol, well specified, with its errors
handled, is worth more here than an ambitious one that half works. If
your implementation is too complex, we may penalize it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Make your image public"}
A package pushed to GitHub Container Registry starts **private**. Make
it public as in
[chapter 05](../chapters/05-docker.qmd#publishing-to-the-github-container-registry):
**Package settings** > **Danger Zone** > **Change visibility** >
**Public**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="How and what to present"}
Present your work as you like: slides, a live demo, a poster. But:

- no need to repeat the objectives, we know them.
- no need to walk through the code, unless a part of it is interesting,
  complex or tricky.
- focus on the **what** and the **why**.

Aim at someone who knows the course but has never heard of your
project.
:::

    information.

[^explicit-error-messages]: Explicit error messages clearly explain what
    went wrong and how to fix it. They are user-friendly and easy to
    understand.
